anatomy.intro: A branching, flexible outline explains why a young upright pot can eventually need more room.

parts.function: The green cylindrical stem carries a series of low ribs.
parts.label: Slender stem

parts.function: Small felted growing cushions sit closely together along the ribs.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: Fine pale-to-brown spines radiate from the areoles.
parts.label: Radial spines

parts.function: A new branch adds another extending stem to the scrambling plant.
parts.label: Side branch

flowers.text: The classical description records white flowers roughly 15–19 cm long, emerging near the upper areoles, followed by red fruit. A potential bloom is much broader than the thin stem that bears it; flowering has not been recorded for this collection specimen.

growth.note: A leaning mature stem can be consistent with its habit; sudden softness or a damaged base is a separate observation.

stages.text: Young stems can stand upright in a compact group.
stages.title: Upright start

stages.text: Longer stems branch and begin to lean or arch.
stages.title: Extending branches

stages.text: With age, stems can clamber through supports or trail when unsupported.
stages.title: Scrambling adult

habitat.text: Serpent cactus is native to Mexico, where Kew describes it as a scrambling succulent shrub of seasonally dry tropical habitats. Its slender stems are built for a different life from a compact barrel cactus: the classic botanical description records stems climbing through bushes, trailing over walls or hanging when support is absent.

Exactly four large circled numbered markers 1-4 with clear thin leaders pointing to the features specified below in order. Numbers legible at 350px display width. No words, title, paragraphs, watering or calendar icons. No pot, roots, flowers or grafts unless explicitly requested. Nyctocereus serpentinus, serpent cactus: a rooted-looking cluster shown without roots of several slender cylindrical green cactus stems; taller stems lean and arch gracefully, one side branch emerges naturally. No flowers.

lookalikes.name: Ming Thing
lookalikes.text: Both are cacti, but Ming Thing grows in thick irregular clubs. Serpent cactus develops long, comparatively slender ribbed stems and a scrambling habit; its branches are not flat cactus pads.

mature.text: Stems in the botanical description can reach around 3 m long while remaining only about 2–5 cm thick. Those dimensions describe developed plants, not a growth promise for the indoor pot.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Costa Farms.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: Kew currently accepts Nyctocereus serpentinus and lists Peniocereus serpentinus as a synonym. Finding either name in a reference does not by itself indicate a different plant.

sources.title: Britton and Rose — The Cactaceae, volume 2
